Read what an Olympus recorder wrote about a recording

Source: R/olym.R
olym.Rd

Reads the olym chunks of a wave file. Olympus recorders write one into every file they make, holding the model of the recorder, the number the recording was given on it, the time it was started and the time it was ended, how long it runs, and any marks that were put in it while it was being made.

Usage

olym(x)

Arguments

x

Path to a wave file, a Wave object with olym metadata attached, a raw vector holding a wave file, or an olym object

Value

An olym object, which is a named list of the fields the chunk held: model, fileNumber, timestamp, timestampEnd, recordingTime and duration in seconds, marks in seconds from the start of the recording, and text and text.2. A file holding more than one olym chunk gives the fields of the second under names ending in a further number.

Details

The chunk is commonly the only metadata such a file carries: a wave file out of an LS or DM recorder has no INFO list, no broadcast metadata and no tag, and before this chunk was read there was nothing in it for this package to find.

duration and recordingTime are two ways the recorder wrote the same thing, the first in milliseconds and the second to the second, and across the 397 files in the corpora they never disagree. Neither is the length of the audio the file now holds: 307 of the 397 agree with the data chunk to within half a second, and of the 90 that do not, 89 say the recording was longer than the audio that is there, which is what a file cut after it came off the recorder looks like.

timestampEnd is not the time the audio ends either. It is the time the recorder stopped, which includes however long it was paused for: in 152 of the 397 it is further from the start than the recording is long, by as much as thirteen hours.

Two fields hold a hundred characters of text each, and nothing documents what either is for. One file of the 397 writes in them, putting the subject of the recording in the second, so they are read and reported under the names text and text.2, by the slot they came from rather than by any meaning, and neither is taken for the title of the recording.

See also

readMetadata() reads this and every other metadata format a file carries at once, and wavCues() reads the marks an editor wrote into a recording afterwards, which the recorder's own marks are separate from.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
olym("recording.wav")
} # }
